title: A globular cluster’s striking red eye
caption: The globular cluster NGC 2108, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2108 · constellation Dorado · about 150000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A gleaming ruby-red spot sits at the center left of this colorful globular cluster, like a watchful eye. The cluster is NGC 2108, which sits inside the Large Magellanic Cloud, in the direction of Dorado, the Swordfish.

That red eye is in fact a carbon star, a type of star that is nearly always a cool red giant with an atmosphere containing more carbon than oxygen, the reverse of the Sun. In the star's outer layer, carbon and oxygen join up as carbon monoxide until the oxygen runs out.

The leftover carbon is then free to build other compounds, including molecules such as C2, CH and CN. These molecules scatter blue light inside the star while letting red light pass through, which is why the star glows such a deep red among its neighbors.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.25 x 2.59 arcminutes) and distance (150000 light years), the frame spans roughly 142 × 113 light-years. Its light set out about 150,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys captured the cluster through three filters, blue, visual and near-infrared. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves the individual stars of a cluster that lies in another galaxy.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: John Herschel, astronomer, mathematician, chemist and inventor, and son of William Herschel, discovered the cluster in 1835. It lies about 150,000 light-years away.
alt: A colorful globular cluster with a bright ruby-red star at the center left.
